title: How AI helps brokers grow: a conversation with Outsail
summary: Our CEO, Pauline Roteta, sat down with Outsail to discuss how brokers can grow their book with AI.
body_markdown:
A brokerage grows when its people have time to consult with clients. For most of the year, that time goes to manual work. Renewal season means chasing carriers for quotes and lining up the plans in a spreadsheet. Then enrollment starts, and the same plan details have to be written into different systems, a benefits guide, and every email that goes to employees.


AI can now take on a lot of that document work, which changes the question a brokerage has to answer. It used to be how to get through the season. Now it's what to do with the hours that come back, because those hours are where new clients and new commissions come from.


Our CEO, Pauline Roteta, sat down on Zoom to talk this through with Brett Ungashick, founder of[OutSail](https://www.outsail.co/) , a firm that helps employers choose their HR software.


## Why the work for brokers take so long


We know this work because we used to do it by hand. Pasito started with a decision support product for employees, and setting up each employer meant reading plan PDFs hundreds of pages long and building the plan design, rates, and eligibility rules ourselves. After doing this enough times by hand, we started using AI on our own work. We taught models to read carrier proposals, reformat census files, and draft benefits communications. Those foundational tools are what we later brought to brokerages and carriers.


What we saw then is still true. Plan details start at the carrier and get re-entered at every step before an employee reads them. The carrier has a quoting system, the brokerage has its own CRM, and the employer has an HR system. None of them share data. An account manager at each stage ends up building the benefits in one program and the enrollment presentation in another from the same numbers, and every re-entry is a chance for an error that an employee will find.


## Start with proposals and enrollment


These two stretches are the place to begin because they're where account managers spend the most time. During renewal season, AI can handle the requests to carriers and the plan comparisons. In enrollment, an account manager can use it to produce the guides, the microsites, and the communication campaigns.


Brokerages that get comfortable there go on to connect the year. The plans chosen in a proposal carry straight into employee education. An AI assistant answers employees' questions after enrollment. What employees ask helps shape the next renewal. No brokerage begins at that point. You start with one part of the work, but as you tally up wins, you can become more ambitious taking processes end to end.


## Where the saved hours go next


Time back only matters if it turns into revenue, and there are three ways that happens.


The first is clients a brokerage couldn't serve before. A brokerage we work with wanted to serve PEOs. A PEO has thousands of client groups where an employer has one, so a benefits guide or a microsite for each of them wasn't possible by hand. With AI doing that work, the brokerage brought in more than $2 million in commissions. The same idea applies to a small-group brokerage building an enterprise practice, or a mid-market brokerage serving small groups at scale.


The second is new lines of coverage. Take long-term care. Long-term care is a product that is significantly more expensive when bought in the individual market, but it's a lot of work (or perceived as a lot of work) for an employer to launch. A brokerage that can run that launch across clients has a new line of revenue.


The third is consulting. Many brokers have ideas for bringing a client's costs down and no time to work on them. With more hours, that work can reach smaller employers too, where service often feels transactional. Bringing costs down is what clients care about most, and it takes time that brokers rarely have during the year.


## The client relationship stays with the broker


None of this replaces the broker. Benefits is a human business. It deals with healthcare and finances, and the relationship a broker has with a client can't be handed to software. AI takes the forms, the documents, and the execution so brokers have more time with clients.


Higher value work means more revenue and more jobs in this industry. We also expect brokerages to pull apart over the next three to five years, between the firms that work this way and the ones that don't. Established brokerages have the advantage, because they already have the relationships.
